title: Why Explosions Look Like This
text: To understand a nuclear explosion in space, we first have to understand why explosions look the way they do on Earth.
nxt: Down here, we live at the bottom of a dense ocean of invisible gas.

title: Why Explosions Look Like This
text: When a nuclear weapon detonates in the atmosphere, roughly half of its energy becomes blast, a mechanical force.
nxt: The bomb heats the surrounding air to tens of millions of degrees.

title: The Shockwave and the Mushroom
text: That wall is the shockwave. It travels faster than sound, tearing through buildings, snapping steel towers, and shattering glass across entire cities.

title: The Shockwave and the Mushroom
text: At the same time, the superheated pocket of air becomes much lighter than the cold air around it.
nxt: It surges upward like a giant balloon, dragging dust, debris, and smoke into a rising stem.

text: When intense X-rays hit a solid surface, physics produces a brutal effect called blow-off impulse.
nxt: The thin outer layer of the spacecraft's skin absorbs so much energy in a fraction of a second that it vaporizes.

title: Starfish Prime

text: The rocket lifted off from Johnston Island, a tiny speck of land in the Pacific.

title: Starfish Prime

title: Lessons and Treaties

title: Lessons and Treaties

nxt: A few years later, the Outer Space Treaty of 1967 barred placing nuclear weapons in orbit.
